articles.title: 24 Check Point servers were breached. I built a CLI that counts how many days overdue your KEV patches are.
articles.excerpt: 24 Check Point servers were breached. I built a CLI that counts how many days overdue your KEV patches are. On 23 November 2026, GreyNoise published its report on GT13: a campaign that compromised 24…
articles.body: 24 Check Point servers were breached. I built a CLI that counts how many days overdue your KEV patches are. On 23 November 2026, GreyNoise published its report on GT13: a campaign that compromised 24 Check Point Security Management servers across at least 22 organisations in 17 countries. The activity ran from 17 October to 2 November 2026, with the first sighting on 2 October. The attackers ran more than 1,400 sessions, dropped 800+ CLI artifacts and 1,200+ files, and on 26 October attempted a bulk certificate-management task across all 24 servers at once. It failed - but the campaign had already been running for weeks.

articles.title: Stacking add-on licenses on one install
articles.excerpt: A customer buys the base edition of your product. Six months later they buy an add-on pack that unlocks three more modules, and your fulfilment pipeline delivers it as a second signed key — not a reis…
articles.body: A customer buys the base edition of your product. Six months later they buy an add-on pack that unlocks three more modules, and your fulfilment pipeline delivers it as a second signed key — not a reissue of the first. Now the installation holds two Keyright licenses at once. Next quarter an enterprise account stacks a site license with a per-seat top-up, and that is three. Your IsEnabled("analytics") was written against a single LicenseInfo . What does it even mean to ask whether a feature is enabled when the answer is spread across several independently-signed grants with different expiries — and one of them has just been revoked? The instinct is to pick one license as "primary" and treat the rest as patches. That instinct is wrong, and it gets worse every time you add a rule.

articles.body: Countdown timers in React are where setInterval goes to die. The interval keeps ticking after the round ends, the UI updates with stale values, and the cleanup you forgot turns into a memory leak. This challenge replaces that pattern with a self-rescheduling setTimeout that you own from start to finish. 🧩 Overview Build a 10-round timed globe-guessing game: a country is highlighted in red on a 3D globe and you have 15 seconds to name it. It's a small game that drills three things you use in every app — effect cleanup, countdown timers, and resetting state between rounds. 👉 https://www.reactchallenges.com/challenges/country-guess ✅ Requirements Implement the game in App.tsx .

articles.title: Read income, spending and profit together — not sales alone
articles.excerpt: A busy month can still leave very little behind. Sales alone do not tell you that — spending does. In my November 2026 income and expense sample, the three numbers read together: income 40,640,000 VND…
articles.body: A busy month can still leave very little behind. Sales alone do not tell you that — spending does. In my November 2026 income and expense sample, the three numbers read together: income 40,640,000 VND, spending 29,880,000 VND, profit 10,760,000 VND. Looking only at the first number makes the month look stronger than it is; the third number is the one that says what actually stayed. Two habits keep the three numbers honest: record each transaction on the day it happens, one row at a time, so nothing is rebuilt from memory at month end; and read income, spending and profit on the same screen before deciding what to buy next month. Do you check your profit number every month, or only your sales? Disclosure: this post was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author.

articles.title: The repo was Apache-2.0. The model it downloaded at runtime had no license at all.
articles.excerpt: In July I was planning a small commercial tool that turns a single character illustration into a layered, rig-ready file. The heavy lifting was going to come from an open-source research project I'd f…
articles.body: In July I was planning a small commercial tool that turns a single character illustration into a layered, rig-ready file. The heavy lifting was going to come from an open-source research project I'd found on GitHub. It did what I needed on straightforward full-body characters, although it struggled with a voluminous costume and with a character whose face was hidden. The repository had an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file at the top level. I almost stopped checking there. I'm glad I didn't, because the part of that project that actually produced the output wasn't covered by that file at all. One of the two models its inference script downloads at runtime had no license of any kind. Not a restrictive license. Not a non-commercial license. Nothing.

articles.title: Jira Plans Auto Schedule vs a Gantt Drag Review
articles.excerpt: Jira Plans, Atlassian's planning feature in the Premium and Enterprise plans, auto-schedules work and then holds the new dates in the plan until you save it through Review changes. LeanZero Management…
articles.body: Jira Plans, Atlassian's planning feature in the Premium and Enterprise plans, auto-schedules work and then holds the new dates in the plan until you save it through Review changes. LeanZero Management, our Gantt and planning app for Jira Cloud, does the same for one drag. On our demo plan one drag moved 18 work items and staged 19 date changes. Jira got none of them. The review lists each date, old one struck through. Review with AI then checks the plan before you write anything: first with checks the app computes itself, then with an AI that reads up to 120 of the plan's work items. People ask to lose that review step.

articles.title: November's full moon dazzles skywatchers with a stunning Beaver Moon supermoon (photos)
articles.excerpt: From the skyscrapers of New York to the ancient Parthenon in Athens, the Beaver Moon supermoon put on a spectacular show for skywatchers around the world.
articles.body: The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov. 24 and we've got the photos to prove it! Read on to see our favorite shots of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world. Each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names , often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising. The November moon is often known as the Beaver Moon, a name associated with the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and when trappers historically set beaver traps before waterways froze. November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons , which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.

articles.title: SpaceX launches secretive spy satellites from California for US Space Force (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched its fifth classified mission for U.S. national security this month today (Nov. 24), from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
articles.body: SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT) , carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month. While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space .
